newsitem.title: EL SALVADOR: Ex-guerrillas make big gains in El Salvador vote.
newsitem.headline: Ex-guerrillas make big gains in El Salvador vote.

text.p: El Salvador's Farabundo Marti National Liberation Front (FMLN) posted big gains in mid-term elections, winning at the ballot box what the ex-guerrillas failed to gain on the battlefield, officials said on Monday.

The leftist FMLN was nearly even with the ruling right-wing party in the overall vote, picking up a solid block of seats in Congress, and seemed to have sewn up the mayoral race for the capital city of San Salvador, official results showed.

Salvadoran voters appeared to deal a blow to the ruling Republican National Alliance (ARENA), which had been an electoral juggernaut since the late 1980s at the height of El Salvador's civil war, the bloodiest in Central America at that time.
With 58.6 percent of the vote counted, ARENA was polling 35.4 percent of the total vote, just above the FMLN's 34.2 percent, the Supreme Electoral Tribunal (TSE) said on Monday.
In the raw count ARENA had 238,140 votes to the FMLN's 230,542.

"The Salvadoran people, apparently even at the national level, have decided to try an adventure. I think that the adventure will be dangerous, but if it is the will of the people we are going to respect it," Mario Valiente, ARENA party leader and current mayor of San Salvador, told a news conference.

Mortal enemies backed by the Cold War superpowers little more than five years ago, the FMLN and ARENA on Sunday far surpassed nine smaller parties in races for all 84 seats in Congress and 262 municipalities.
Turnout was low as about 40 percent of the 2.6 million eligible voters showed up at the polls. The tribunal declared the voting transparent and there were no serious allegations of irregularities.

FMLN leaders claimed they would pick up a minimum of 29 seats in Congress and possibly as many as 35. In any event they will improve on their current total of 20, and ARENA's total of 39 seats will fall.

In addition, ARENA conceded the race for mayor of San Salvador to the former guerrillas, who ran in a coalition with two smaller parties, winning 48.8 percent or 38,027 votes to 40.6 percent or 33,033 votes for ARENA with just under 60 percent of the ballots counted.
"I am ready to govern," Hector Silva, 49, the FMLN mayoral candidate, told reporters.
In the 1980s, the FMLN was widely considered Latin America's most professional guerrilla army, held at bay by billions of dollars in U.S. aid that bolstered the Salvadoran armed forces.

But after signing a peace treaty with ex-President Alfredo Cristiani of ARENA in 1992, the former rebels stumbled in their first elections in 1994 and President Armando Calderon Sol swept to victory by nearly a two-to-one margin over the FMLN-backed candidate.
ARENA leaders acknowledged the gains by the FMLN in Sunday's vote.

"We recognise that the preliminary results indicate that we had not maintained a quantity of deputies and mayors," said Gloria Salguero, president of the ARENA in the Legislative Assembly as the unicameral Congress is known.
Voting took place in an atmosphere of calm under the watchful eye of about 10,000 police and 1,000 international observers.
"The best proof of transparency in an election is when the opposition wins," Pedro Monterosa, an alternate magistrate on the Supreme Electoral Tribunal, told reporters.
